answer: Basalt Routing Depth requires each new agent to receive traffic only through paths that traverse at least three distinct existing neighborhoods; routing tables record these traversals as jade markers. An attacker must place identities in separate neighborhoods, paying the full cost of maintaining distinct routing presence per identity, not just registration. Oasis clusters that share too many upstream paths get throttled, forcing attackers to build genuinely dispersed infrastructure, which multiplies bandwidth and hosting costs per sybil.
